questions.question: A designer proves her two-gate library can realize every 4-row truth table by first simulating NOT and then AND. Which property has she established for the operator set?
questions.explanation: Functional completeness means the operators can express all Boolean functions; with NOT plus one of AND/OR every truth function is constructible.

questions.question: A binary connective written p↑q is false only when both inputs are true — and, being functionally complete alone, was chosen to build a minimal-chipset CPU. Name this connective.
questions.explanation: p↑q ≡ ¬(p∧q) is NAND, the Sheffer stroke: false exactly at (T,T), and functionally complete on its own.

questions.question: A binary connective written p↓q is true only when both inputs are false. Like its dual ↑, it alone can express every Boolean function. Name this connective.
questions.explanation: p↓q ≡ ¬(p∨q) is NOR, the Peirce arrow: true only at (F,F), and also functionally complete by itself.

questions.question: A truth-functional reading of 'if the build fails, the alert fires' makes the conditional false in exactly one row: build failed, no alert fired. What is this truth-functional conditional operator called?
questions.explanation: Material implication p→q is false only when p is true and q is false — the truth-functional if-then.

questions.question: The connective in p↔q is true exactly when both sides share a truth value, since it abbreviates (p→q)∧(q→p). By which name is this connective also known?
questions.explanation: p↔q — the biconditional, or material equivalence — holds exactly when p and q have equal truth values.

questions.question: Dualizing the identity p∧(p∨q) ≡ p means replacing every connective and constant: ∧ becomes its dual connective. Which operator replaces ∧?
questions.explanation: The dual of conjunction is disjunction, giving the dual absorption law p∨(p∧q) ≡ p.

questions.question: A simplifier must remove every implication from ¬q→p. Applying x→y ≡ ¬x∨y and cleaning up, which disjunction results?
questions.explanation: ¬q→p ≡ ¬¬q∨p ≡ q∨p: the conditional is eliminated in favor of a plain disjunction.

questions.question: Simplify (p∧(p∨q))∨(p∧q) to a single literal by applying the absorption law twice.
questions.explanation: First absorption gives p∧(p∨q) ≡ p; then p∨(p∧q) ≡ p by the dual absorption law, so the whole formula reduces to p.

questions.question: A minimalist gate library must realize all 16 two-variable Boolean functions while stocking only two operator types. Give one such minimal two-element set.
questions.explanation: {AND, NOT} suffices: p∨q ≡ ¬(¬p∧¬q), and →, ↔, ⊕ are all built from ∧, ∨, ¬. {OR, NOT} works dually.

questions.question: A spec requires 'exactly one of the two inputs may be high'; an engineer wires an OR gate and the test case p=1, q=1 fails. Which connective should replace OR?
questions.explanation: Inclusive OR is true at (1,1), but the spec forbids both inputs high; exclusive OR is false exactly when both inputs are true.

questions.question: Express p⊕q using only AND, OR, and NOT.
alternatives: (p or q) and not(p and q)
questions.explanation: XOR holds when exactly one operand is true: p and not-q, or not-p and q.

questions.question: How many distinct Boolean functions of two variables exist?
questions.explanation: Four input rows each allow two outputs, giving 2^4 = 16 truth functions.

questions.question: Express ¬p using only the NAND operator.
questions.explanation: ¬(p∧p) = ¬p, so feeding the same input to both NAND terminals negates it.

questions.question: How many NAND operations are needed to implement p∧q?
questions.explanation: p∧q = (p NAND q) NAND (p NAND q): one NAND plus a NAND-inverter.

questions.question: Which standard logical operator is self-dual, i.e. f(¬p) = ¬f(p)?
questions.explanation: ¬(¬p) = ¬(¬p): negation equals its own dual, unlike AND and OR which are duals of each other.

questions.question: A circuit computes x = p NAND q, y = p NOR p (a wired inverter), and outputs x AND y. What is the output for p=True, q=False?
XOR gates are cascaded as (p⊕q)⊕r, which computes odd parity. With p=True, q=True, r=True, what is the output?
questions.explanation: T⊕T = F, then F⊕T = T — three true inputs give odd parity, so the output is true.

questions.question: Evaluate (p NAND q) NOR (p NAND q) for p=False with q arbitrary.
questions.explanation: NAND with a false input always outputs T, so both NOR inputs are T; T NOR T = ¬(T∨T) = F.

questions.question: A half-adder outputs sum = p⊕q and carry = p∧q. For inputs p=1, q=1, what two-bit binary number do the (carry, sum) outputs form?
questions.explanation: 1⊕1 = 0 for the sum bit and 1∧1 = 1 for the carry: 1+1 = binary 10.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of NOR gates needed to implement p∧q?
questions.explanation: p∧q = ¬(¬p∨¬q) = (p NOR p) NOR (q NOR q): two NOR-inverters plus a final NOR.
